findings.title: Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates `queue.Queue()` with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never blocks or signals arroyo to pause (poll() only emits a gauge). The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing fills up. If processing falls behind (the exact scenario this PR is meant to handle — a slow item backlogging a queue), arroyo will keep polling and submitting, and in-memory WorkItems accumulate without bound, risking OOM in the consumer process. Either bound the queues and block/reject submit, or expose a pause/resume mechanism to arroyo.

findings.title: Rebalance permanently kills the shared queue pool, silently dropping messages
findings.body: The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. But SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() (queue_consumer.py lines 335-345) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every queue. Arroyo calls join()/close() on the old strategy on every rebalance, then calls create_with_partitions again — the new strategy gets the same, now-dead pool. Subsequent submits will raise queue.ShutDown when putting items; that exception is caught by the generic except in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which marks the offset as complete, so the message is silently dropped and its offset committed. The pool must either be created per-strategy, or the strategy must not shut down the shared pool.

findings.title: Processing failures are swallowed and offsets still committed (silent data loss)
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches all exceptions from result_processor, logs them, and unconditionally marks the offset complete in the finally block. The commit loop then commits that offset. A permanently failing result (e.g. a bug triggered by a particular payload) is therefore dropped with no retry, no DLQ, and no metric — only a log line. At minimum this should increment a failure metric so operators can detect silent loss; ideally it should integrate with the existing DLQ policy or a retry path.

findings.title: Offset gaps permanently block commits for a partition
findings.body: get_committable_offsets stops at the first offset not present in all_offsets and never commits past it. Any offset that is never add_offset'ed for a partition (e.g. messages filtered/dropped upstream of this strategy, or offsets below the initial start after a rebalance where another instance committed some and the tracker's last_committed is stale or -1) creates a permanent gap: all later offsets in that partition become uncommittable, all_offsets grows without bound for the life of the process, and the consumer group's committed lag grows indefinitely, triggering rebalances/max-poll-interval expiry on restart. There is no mechanism to advance past a gap or reset state on partition reassignment.

findings.title: OffsetTracker state is not reset on partition reassignment/rebalance
findings.body: The OffsetTracker lives on the shared FixedQueuePool and retains last_committed, all_offsets, and outstanding across rebalances. After a rebalance, create_with_partitions may be invoked with a different partition assignment and the consumer may resume from offsets previously committed by another instance (which can be lower or unrelated to last_committed). If a new message's offset is <= last_committed for that partition, get_committable_offsets returns nothing for it (start = last_committed+1 skips it) and the offset is never committed, stalling that partition's commits. State should be scoped to a strategy/partition assignment lifecycle.

findings.title: hash(str) is randomized across processes
findings.body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on a string, which is salted per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). This is fine for ordering within a single process, but any future design where multiple processes (or a restart mid-flight with different assignment) rely on consistent group→queue mapping would silently break ordering assumptions. Using a stable hash (e.g. zlib.crc32 or hashlib) would make the mapping deterministic and document the intent. Low priority since current usage is per-process.

findings.title: A Sentry transaction is started per message in every worker
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker wraps every single result_processor call in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). At uptime-results throughput this creates an enormous number of transactions (one per Kafka message per worker), which both adds per-message overhead in the hot path and can flood Sentry. The existing code path (ResultProcessor.__call__) already starts a transaction per result, so this doubles transactions per message. Consider a span or sampling.

findings.title: submit() swallows decoder/assert errors and commits offsets for undecodable messages
findings.body: In submit(), any exception (including the `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` failure and decode_payload exceptions) is caught and the offset is immediately marked complete, so the offset is committed even though the message was never processed and no DLQ is involved. This differs from other modes where a decode failure is at least logged with the payload. Combined with the generic ResultProcessor exception swallowing, there are three separate layers of silent-drop with no metric distinguishing 'dropped at decode' from 'dropped at process'.
